Nigeria’s Flamingos will put their growing confidence to the test when they take on Venezuela in the quarter-finals of the 2026 FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup on Sunday, with a place in the last four at stake in Morocco.
Akeem Busari’s side have recovered impressively from their opening-day disappointment to win three consecutive matches, eliminating defending champions DPR Korea and Mexico along the way. Venezuela, meanwhile, arrive with renewed belief after producing one of the round of 16’s biggest surprises by knocking out Germany, who had won all three of their group-stage matches.
The encounter will take place at the Mohammed VI Football Academy, Pitch 4, in Salé, Morocco, with kick-off scheduled for 7:00 p.m. Nigerian time (6:00 p.m. local time).
For Nigeria, victory would secure a place in the semi-finals for the first time since their historic third-place finish at the 2022 edition in India. It would also take the Flamingos to fourregular-time victories in a single edition of the competition, setting a new national record.
The winner will face either China PR or Brazil in the semi-finals, meaning another victory would bring Nigeria one step closer to the final.
Nigeria’s campaign began with a 2-1 defeat to Poland in Group B, leaving the young Nigerians with little room for further mistakes.
Wiktoria Skrzypczak converted a penalty in the 33rd minute before Natalia Skrok extended Poland’s advantage in the 65th minute. Oluebube Umejiaku gave Nigeria hope with a goal in the 79th minute, assisted by Kanyinsola Yusuf, but the Flamingos could not find a late equaliser.

Busari’s team responded with a much-improved performance against Puerto Rico, securing a 2-0 victory to get their campaign back on track. Oluwakemi Adegbuyi opened the scoring in the 25th minute following an assist from Queen Joseph. At the same time, Precious Oscar came off the bench to seal the win in stoppage time after being set up by Umejiaku.
However, their next performance announced Nigeria as a serious contender in the competition.
The Flamingos produced an outstanding display to defeat two-time defending champions DPR Korea 3-1, inflicting a first regulation-time defeat on the Asian side at the tournament in 2,900 days and ending their remarkable 18-match unbeaten run.
Adegbuyi opened the scoring in the 15th minute, with Mary Dunstan providing the assist. Umejiaku doubled Nigeria’s advantage in the 38th minute after being set up by Tosin Rafiu, while Yusuf added a third in the 56th minute. DPR Korea’s Yu Jong-hyang converted a late penalty in the 82nd minute, but Nigeria held on for a memorable victory.
The result secured Nigeria’s passage from Group B with six points, having scored six goals and conceded four in three matches.
The Flamingos carried that momentum into the round of 16, defeating Mexico 2-1 to book their place in the quarter-finals.
Umejiaku broke the deadlock in the 40th minute after Mexico failed to deal with Esther Stephen’s searching pass. At the same time, Dunstan doubled Nigeria’s lead in the 71st minute, finishing after Kanyinsola Yusuf’s cross was only partially cleared.
Emily Delgado scored a late consolation for Mexico in stoppage time, but Nigeria had done enough to progress.
The victory was significant beyond qualification. It gave the Flamingos their third win at Morocco 2026, matching their best return at a single edition of the competition, previously achieved in 2010, 2014 and 2024.
Now, they have a chance to go one step further and reach the semi-finals for the second time in their history.
Venezuela’s journey to the quarter-finals has been less straightforward, but their latest result makes them an opponent Nigeria cannot afford to underestimate.
They finished third in Group D with three points from three matches, recording one victory and two defeats.
Their campaign opened with a 2-0 loss to France before they recovered to defeat Zambia 3-2 in a dramatic encounter.
Zambia took an early lead through Elizabeth Mofya in the fourth minute, but Ariana Ojeda restored parity for Venezuela nine minutes later. Grace Phiri put Zambia back in front in the 54th minute before Orliany Durán levelled the contest in the 63rd minute.
Andrea Suárez then struck deep into stoppage time to secure Venezuela’s only group-stage victory.
Their final group fixture ended in another 2-0 defeat, this time against Japan, leaving them reliant on the third-placed-team qualification route to reach the knockout stage.
However, Venezuela produced their biggest performance of the tournament in the round of 16, defeating Germany 1-0 on 28 October.
Germany entered the knockout stage with a perfect record, having won all three group matches to top Group E with nine points. But Venezuela stunned the European side when Diana Bravo scored in the fifth minute, and they defended their advantage to secure a place in the last eight.
The result underlined their ability to compete against highly rated opposition, even after an inconsistent group campaign.
Nigeria must therefore approach the contest with the same intensity they showed against DPR Korea and Mexico. Venezuela may have finished third in their group, but their elimination of Germany showed they can make life difficult for any opponent.
Venezuela are making another appearance at the FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup after missing several editions, and their progress in Morocco offers a chance to re-establish themselves among the competition’s leading nations.
Their best performance came in 2014, when they reached the semi-finals and eventually finished fourth. They also participated in the 2010 and 2016 editions but failed to qualify for the tournaments in 2018, 2022 and 2024.
Their return to the quarter-finals in Morocco gives them a chance to repeat their 2014 achievement and move closer to a first final appearance.
The victory over Germany will undoubtedly boost their confidence, particularly after the difficulties they faced during the group stage. Nigeria must be ready for a team that has found a way to deliver when the stakes are highest.
Nigeria and Venezuela have never faced each other at the FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup, making Sunday’s quarter-final their first meeting in the competition.
With no previous World Cup encounter to draw lessons from, both teams will have to rely heavily on their performances in Morocco and their coaches’ tactical preparations.
Nigeria have scored eight goals and conceded five across their four matches, while Venezuela have found the net four times and conceded six.
The numbers suggest that the Flamingos have carried a greater attacking threat. Still, Venezuela’s victory over Germany reminds us that knockout football is not always decided by group-stage statistics.
One of Nigeria’s biggest challenges will be finding a way through a Venezuelan defence that has already shown it can protect a narrow advantage against strong opposition.
Their 1-0 victory over Germany was built around an early breakthrough and disciplined defending. If Venezuela adopt a similar approach against the Flamingos, Busari’s players will need patience, intelligent movement and better decision-making in the final third.
Nigeria have shown that goals can come from different areas of the team, with Umejiaku, Dunstan, Adegbuyi and Yusuf all making important contributions during the campaign.
Umejiaku, in particular, has been influential in the knockout stages, scoring against both Mexico and Poland, while Dunstan’s goal against Mexico further demonstrated Nigeria’s ability to get contributions from midfield.
The Flamingos must also be careful not to become frustrated if Venezuela defend deep and restrict the space available in attacking areas. Rushing passes or committing too many players forward could leave them vulnerable to the South Americans’ counter-attacking opportunities.
Another important factor will be the opening goal. Venezuela scored early against Germany and held their lead for the rest of the match. If they take the initiative against Nigeria, the Flamingos could struggle to break down a compact defensive structure.
At the other end, Nigeria must remain alert whenever possession is lost. Venezuela have already demonstrated their ability to punish opponents, and the Flamingos cannot afford the defensive lapses that proved costly against Poland.
Goalkeeper Jane Ijirigho will also have an important role to play if the South Americans create clear chances, while Nigeria’s attackers must make theirs count.
Ultimately, the contest could be decided by which team handles the crucial moments better. Nigeria have the momentum, attacking confidence and experience of overcoming the defending champions, but Venezuela have earned their place in the quarter-finals and will not be intimidated.
For Busari and his Flamingos, the mission is clear: overcome Venezuela, secure a place in the final four and keep Nigeria’s dream of winning the 2026 FIFA U-17 Women’s World Cup alive.
